item_title: New paper in Nature Climate Change on rhizosphere carbon retention
item_introduction: Michael Carter and co-authors model deep-soil carbon under intensified alpine temperature oscillations.

add_image.image_caption: Soil cores from the rhizosphere carbon study

add_paragraph: A new study published today in ==Nature Climate Change== reveals that rhizosphere carbon retention in alpine soils is far more sensitive to **temperature oscillation patterns** than previously understood.

The research, led by {Michael Carter|mailto:michael.carter@bioterra-lab.org}, uses a novel combination of **isotope tracing**, `metagenomic sequencing`, and high-frequency soil temperature monitoring to trace carbon flow from living roots into stable mineral-associated pools.

The study leverages the lab's decade-long warming experiment at **Storglombreen**, where soil temperatures have been manipulated at 2°C increments across 48 plots since 2016. By introducing ¹³C-labeled root exudates and tracking their fate, the team discovered that increased temperature variability — not just mean warming — **accelerates carbon loss** from the rhizosphere by up to 37%.
The findings have significant implications for Earth system models, which currently parameterize soil carbon feedbacks based on mean annual temperature alone.

images.image_caption: Soil core extraction at warming experiment plots

add_paragraph: The team hopes these results will inform the next generation of Earth system models ahead of the IPCC AR7 cycle. ==Funding== was provided by the National Science Foundation under award #EAR-241558.
